clue.text: Precious 11

definitions.meaning: an endearment for a loved one, like sweetheart or dear
the 11-across theme: Alistair ... held that Treasury post from 2007 to 2010

explanation.surface: A cross-reference that reads like a cherished number eleven, perhaps a favourite footballer.
explanation.walkthrough: 11 points to 11-across, the theme: Chancellors of the Exchequer, the UK finance minister.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses fit: a term of endearment for someone precious, and the surname of a Labour Chancellor of the Exchequer.

clue.text: Replace tape with superb content

indicators.note: to re-place is to put in a different position, so the letters of tape are rearranged

parts.note: ace is slang for excellent or superb

explanation.surface: An instruction to swap a cassette for something of better quality.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Replace' reads as 'swap', but split as re-place it is the anagram signal. 'Content' looks like a noun (what the tape holds) but is the adjective meaning satisfied.
explanation.definitionFit: Being content means being calm and untroubled, the same untroubled state as the phrase describing tranquillity.

clue.text: Draw wasted, having blown lead

indicators.note: the word has lost its leading letter, which is blown away

parts.note: blotto is slang for very drunk, as is wasted

explanation.surface: A drunk gambler loses the lead in a game or contest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having blown lead' takes the first letter B off BLOTTO.
explanation.definitionFit: A lottery is a draw of numbered tickets or balls, and the national game is commonly called by this short name.

clue.text: Hanger-on collared, having kissed the first person to speak?

indicators.note: these words signal that the words are said out loud and heard as another word

parts.note: to neck is to kiss and cuddle, so kissed gives necked; I is the first person singular pronoun

explanation.surface: A clingy companion gets grabbed by the collar after stealing a kiss from someone.
explanation.walkthrough: Said aloud, 'necked I' runs together into the answer. 'Hanger-on' sounds like a clingy person, but here it means something that literally hangs from a collar.
explanation.definitionFit: A tie hangs down from the shirt collar it is knotted around, so it is literally something hanging on a collar.

clue.text: Hypocrisy to embrace as a game

indicators.note: one word holds another inside it, as arms hug a person

parts.note: cant is insincere, pious talk, i.e. hypocrisy
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone's hypocrisy is treated as nothing more than a game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as a game' reads as one phrase, but 'as' is fodder and 'game' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a rummy-style card game, of Uruguayan origin, played with two packs.

clue.text: Gather together a team for conference

indicators.note: a conference is a talk, so the phrase is heard when spoken rather than seen

parts.note: a crew is a team, as of rowers or sailors

explanation.surface: Assemble a squad to attend a conference.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a crew' spoken sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To accumulate is to build up gradually, as interest or benefits gather together over time.

clue.text: Rugby team, seven of whom tackling fifty

indicators.note: in rugby to tackle is to grab hold of a player, so one piece is grabbed and held inside another

parts.note: a rugby union side of fifteen fields seven backs, so seven of them are all backs
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: Seven players from a rugby side bring down someone fifty times over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seven of whom' reads as 'all backs': in rugby union seven of the fifteen players are backs. 'tackling' puts L inside.
explanation.definitionFit: The New Zealand national rugby union side is famous for its all-black strip, which gives it its nickname.

clue.text: Beat gutless tiger, wild cat

indicators.note: with its insides removed only the outermost letters of the word tiger stay

parts.note: the ounce is the snow leopard, a wild cat of Central Asia

explanation.surface: A cowardly tiger is beaten by a fierce wildcat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gutless' sounds like cowardice but takes the inside out of TIGER, leaving TR.
explanation.definitionFit: To thrash or defeat soundly is to beat, as in a sporting rout.

clue.text: Elusive fast animal now, the thylacine

indicators.note: something elusive slips away and won't stay put, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A quick animal that is now very hard to find: the thylacine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Elusive' rearranges FAST ANIMAL NOW. The surface is apt: the thylacine is thought extinct, so 'elusive... now' is literally true.
explanation.definitionFit: The thylacine was a striped carnivorous marsupial of Tasmania, also called the Tasmanian tiger, last seen in captivity in 1936.

clue.text: Reversible lids to identify

indicators.note: it signals that the word can be turned round and read backwards

parts.note: tops are lids, as on jars

explanation.surface: Lids that can be turned inside out, used for labelling something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reversible' turns TOPS back to front.
explanation.definitionFit: To spot something is to pick it out or recognise it, the same as identifying it.

clue.text: Record returns by coincidence for the one at this number?

indicators.note: here it means next to, so the record piece goes beside the coincidence piece

parts.note: chance is accident or coincidence

indicators.note: it signals that the word for record comes back the other way

parts.note: a roll is an official list or record, as an electoral roll

explanation.surface: A record comes back purely by coincidence for whoever lives at this address.
explanation.walkthrough: 'this number' is the clue's own number, 11: No 11 Downing Street is the official residence of the UK's finance minister.
explanation.definitionFit: The Chancellor of the Exchequer lives at 11 Downing Street, so the clue's number is that minister's address.

clue.text: Pound value, everyone can see a loss for 11

parts.note: L, from Latin libra, is the abbreviation for the pound sterling

indicators.note: it signals that a letter goes missing from the word for value

parts.note: an amount is a sum or value
U is the British film certificate for universal viewing, so anyone may watch

explanation.surface: The pound's value is falling, with a loss everyone can see, for the Treasury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a loss' takes U from AMOUNT, leaving AMONT. Norman Lamont was Chancellor when the pound left the Exchange Rate Mechanism in 1992, so the surface fits.
explanation.definitionFit: Norman Lamont was Chancellor of the Exchequer under John Major from 1990 to 1993.

clue.text: 11 tearful guy, primarily

parts.note: maudlin means tearfully sentimental

indicators.note: it signals that just the first letter of the next word is used

explanation.surface: A weepy man described in a few words, as if writing about a sad chancellor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'primarily' takes G, the first letter of 'guy'.
explanation.definitionFit: Reginald Maudling was Chancellor of the Exchequer from 1962 to 1964, under Macmillan and Douglas-Home.

clue.text: Common scruff in poet, son moving away!

indicators.note: one piece goes inside the other
the son leaves home, so that word is taken out of the poet's name

parts.note: Alfred, Lord Tennyson was the Victorian Poet Laureate
taken as written
the scruff of the neck is the nape

explanation.surface: An ordinary scruffy poet whose son has left home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scruff' suggests untidiness, but the scruff of the neck is its back.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that is ten a penny is so plentiful it is cheap and everyday, i.e. common.

clue.text: Sound gathering way below walls in retrospect in creative space

indicators.note: one piece gathers others up inside it

parts.note: audio means sound, as in audio equipment

indicators.note: in a down answer, below means the way piece comes after the walls piece
walls are a thing's outside edges, so the outer letters of the next word are taken

parts.note: ST, short for street, is a way

explanation.surface: Soundproofing gathered under the walls, looking back at a creative room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in retrospect' looks like an instruction to look back, but 'walls in' picks the outer letters of 'retrospect', with nothing turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: A studio for painters or sculptors is a workroom set aside for making things, a creative space.

clue.text: Stitch up something with a thread

definitions.meaning: to stitch someone up is to cheat or swindle them, to do the dirty on them
a metal fastener with a spiral ridge running round it

explanation.surface: Sewing something with a needle and thread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stitch up' and 'thread' suggest sewing, but one is slang for cheating and the other is a spiral ridge.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for cheating someone, and the threaded metal fastener driven in by turning.

clue.text: Capital left, nothing

parts.note: quit can mean left, departed
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Someone walked away with no money left at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' reads as money but is a capital city.
explanation.definitionFit: Quito is the capital city of Ecuador, high in the Andes.

clue.text: Former tennis champion in America, inept

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: US, the United States
Monica Seles won nine Grand Slam singles titles in the 1990s

explanation.surface: A former tennis star turns out to be hopeless in America.
explanation.walkthrough: Seles became a US citizen, so 'in America' fits the surface too.
explanation.definitionFit: Inept and incompetent people are of no use, so the synonym is good-for-nothing or ineffective.

clue.text: Punching the puncher, soldier as Walter Mitty?

indicators.note: it signals that the following words go inside, punching into the puncher

parts.note: a fist is what does the punching
a soldier ant is a worker caste of ant
taken as written

explanation.surface: A daydreamer imagines himself as a soldier in a fist fight.
explanation.walkthrough: Walter Mitty, from James Thurber's story, daydreams of heroic exploits; the question mark marks him as an example of the type.
explanation.definitionFit: Thurber's Walter Mitty is the type of the daydreamer who lives in a fantasy of heroism, an example.

clue.text: Cry on seeing a fox, but trapping friend

indicators.note: one piece holds the other inside it, as a trap does

parts.note: tho, short for though, means but
an ally is a friend

explanation.surface: A huntsman sees a fox and shouts, yet a friend is caught too.
explanation.walkthrough: 'but' gives an informal, shortened spelling of 'though'.
explanation.definitionFit: Fox hunters shout this as the cry when the quarry is sighted, a traditional hunting call.

clue.text: Oddly sorry about 11, as wet

indicators.note: one piece goes round the other
it means only the odd-numbered letters of sorry are taken

parts.note: Geoffrey Howe was Chancellor of the Exchequer from 1979 to 1983

explanation.surface: Someone apologises strangely to the Chancellor for being feeble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wet' is Thatcher-era slang for a weak Tory, which Howe was called, but here it means rainy.
explanation.definitionFit: Showery weather brings rain on and off, so it is wet in short bursts.

clue.text: Endless fury, over and over, for application under pressure

indicators.note: it takes the last letter off the word for fury

parts.note: ire is anger or fury
on can mean over, as in a lid on a box
a second on, again meaning over

explanation.surface: Fury that goes on and on is applied under pressure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endless' cuts IRE to IR; 'over and over' gives ON twice.
explanation.definitionFit: Iron-on patches or transfers are designed to be fixed by pressing with a hot iron.

clue.text: Old Tory contention, where migrants may be entering Britain

definitions.text: where migrants may be entering Britain

parts.note: Edward Heath was the Conservative prime minister from 1970 to 1974
a row is a dispute or contention

explanation.surface: An old Conservative is arguing over immigration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'migrants' suggests immigration, but includes travellers and birds.
explanation.definitionFit: London's busiest airport is a main point of arrival into Britain for people coming from abroad.

clue.text: Rules working for 11

parts.note: laws are rules
on means working, as a machine that is switched on

explanation.surface: Rules that work in favour of the theme minister.
explanation.definitionFit: Nigel Lawson was Chancellor of the Exchequer under Margaret Thatcher from 1983 to 1989.

clue.text: Pledge to bag Lancashire's opener, as a great spinner

indicators.note: to bag something is to catch and hold it, so one piece holds another

parts.note: to give your word is to pledge

indicators.note: the opener of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A promise to dismiss a Lancashire opening batter, from a great spin bowler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'opener' and 'spinner' suggest cricket (Lancashire is an English county side), but the spinner is the Earth.
explanation.definitionFit: The Earth rotates on its axis, so it is a huge spinning body, a whimsical description.

clue.text: Where a test may be sound as a bell in 11

indicators.note: one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: Denis Healey was the Labour Chancellor of the Exchequer from 1974 to 1979
a ding is the noise a bell makes

explanation.surface: An examination may be in perfect order, just as a minister expects.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sound as a bell' reads as 'in perfect health' but is the noise a bell makes. A Test is an international cricket match.
explanation.definitionFit: The Leeds cricket ground hosts Test matches, England's five-day international games.

clue.text: Bird to catch, tail first

indicators.note: the last letter is brought round to the front

parts.note: to catch what someone says is to hear it

explanation.surface: A bird to be caught by grabbing it by the tail first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tail first' moves the R of HEAR to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a large flightless South American bird, similar to the ostrich.

clue.text: 11 from Canberra, might you say?

indicators.note: it signals the words are heard spoken aloud as another word

parts.note: Canberra is in Australia, Oz, so someone from there is Oz-born

explanation.surface: An Australian version of the minister, as one might put it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oz-born' spoken sounds like the name of George Osborne, Chancellor of the Exchequer when this puzzle appeared in 2016.
explanation.definitionFit: George Osborne was Chancellor of the Exchequer under David Cameron from 2010 to 2016.

clue.text: I'm going to depart, body failing, end of life

parts.note: to go is to depart

indicators.note: a failing body breaks down, so its letters are rearranged
it takes just the last letter of the next word

explanation.surface: A dying person's farewell as the body fails at life's end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'failing' rearranges BODY to ODBY; 'end of life' gives E.
explanation.definitionFit: A farewell said on leaving, as someone announces that they are off.
